newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German bank workers protest over sick pay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German bank workers protest over sick pay.

text.p: Around 15,000 German bank employees took to the streets on Friday to protest against cuts in sick payments by employers in one of the largest shows of worker force ever seen in the normally peaceable sector.

The protests included a demonstration by 2,000 workers outside Frankfurt's ornate Alte Oper opera building, where German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and finance ministers from across Europe were speaking at the European Banking Congress.

In the north of the country, trade unions said around 3,000 bank employees in the town of Bremen had embarked on an all-day strike while in Hamburg around 500 workers at Germany's largest commercial bank, Deutsche Bank AG, staged a walk-out.
Further protests took place in around 20 German towns, including Cologne, Hanover, Munich, Berlin and Leipzig, with a total of 40,000 participants expected by the end of the day.

The industrial action follows a new law allowing employers to cut sick pay from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent, and comes after mass protests last month in Germany's metal, engineering and chemical industries.
The banking and insurance union HBV warned that further protests were likely if the banks did not reverse the cuts and continue to pay sick entitlements at full salary.
"If we are forced to, we will take hundreds of thousands of workers on to the streets to bring the employers to their senses," HBV member Klaus Carlin told a news briefing.

Chancellor Kohl, whose government introduced the sick pay cuts in September as part of an austerity plan aimed at speeding Germany towards the single European currency, had earlier come under personal attack in demonstrations.
"Kohl must go!" protestors at the European Banking Congress shouted while littering the streets of Germany's banking capital with cabbage heads. The German word for cabbage is "Kohl".
Union officials said the walk-outs had upset banking business around the country and Bremen walk-outs in particular caused "severe disruption" to Deutsche Bank's operations there.
But a Deutsche Bank spokesman denied business had been hit and said it continued to back the cuts. "There has been no effect at all on our business," the spokesman said by telephone.
Worsening relations in the German banking sector, which has not seen widespread industrial action since 1992, comes as the major banks are seeking to win more business by extending opening hours.

Aside from Deutsche, most of the large banks including Dresdner Bank and Commerzbank AG have already implemented the new law, which they say will help them to shave millions of marks off their personnel costs.
But Gerhard Renner, chief negotiator at the DAG white collar workers union, said the savings a large bank could make through the cuts in proportion to profits were insignificant.

"Deutsche Bank's nine month (operating) profit was over three billion marks for the first nine months of the year. In contrast, this cut will save it just 23 million marks ($15.3 million) in a whole year," Renner said.
He warned bank managers that as a result of the cuts there was now "even less readiness" among employees to work overtime hours necessary for banks to extend their opening hours.

Banking unions say that while current wage contracts in the sector do not specifically cover sick pay at 100 percent of salary, the move to cut sick pay is unjustified and unnecessary because of the low absenteeism in the industry.
Union leaders said they would be ready to bring forward to December or January negotiations with employers on the 1997 wage round in order to find a solution to the sick pay dispute.
